title: Avalanches can increase stored energy in a granular fault
authors: A. Douin, E. Saurety, V. Levy dit Vehel, L. Combe, L. Vanel, O. Cochet-Escartin, O. Ramos
abstract: Slowly sheared granular materials generally store mechanical energy and dilate between abrupt failures that release energy and compact the material. Here, simultaneous measurements of torque, layer thickness, acoustic emission, and photoelastic force networks reveal all four combinations of energy release or storage with contraction or dilation in a compressed granular fault. Most strikingly, some avalanches both dilate the layer and increase the elastic energy transmitted to the resisting boundary. These events reorganize force chains beyond the shear band and produce a distinct acoustic response. The results show that an avalanche need not relax a driven disordered material; it can instead redistribute stress into a more highly loaded configuration, a mechanism with potential relevance to the physics of both laboratory and natural faults.
summary: This experimental work examines energy dynamics in a granular fault under slow shearing, finding that some avalanches can paradoxically increase stored elastic energy rather than just dissipating it. By measuring mechanical, acoustic, and force network changes, the authors distinguish between energy-releasing and energy-storing failure modes. This suggests that failure in disordered materials can be a process of stress redistribution rather than simple relaxation.
main_problem: The study investigates whether avalanches in granular faults can increase stored mechanical energy, challenging the conventional view that failure is purely dissipative.
main_result: Avalanches can reorganize stress into a more highly loaded configuration, evidenced by energy-storing events (Q4) that combine dilation with increased elastic energy, suggesting energy storage is possible.
method: The researchers used simultaneous measurements of torque, layer thickness, acoustic emissions, and photoelastic force networks during slow shearing of a granular fault.
model_or_system: The system is a granular fault composed of photoelastic disks confined between fixed walls, subjected to slow, quasi-static shearing and compression.
key_observables: Torque ($\Gamma$), layer thickness ($h$), acoustic emissions, and mechanical energy variations ($\Delta E_{grains}, \Delta E_h$).
important_parameters: Loading rate, confinement geometry, and the classification of avalanche regimes (Q1-Q4).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on energy conservation principles ($\Delta E = \Delta E_{grains} + \Delta E_h$) and quasi-static loading assumptions.
figures_summary: Figures show time series of mechanical and acoustic signals over long experiments, illustrating major energy release and storage events.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes different avalanche regimes (Q1-Q4) by correlating mechanical energy changes, structural rearrangements (force networks), and acoustic signatures to distinguish between energy-releasing and energy-storing failure modes.
why_interesting: The study of energy dissipation and storage in driven, disordered mechanical systems provides an experimental analogue for understanding energy flow and non-equilibrium dynamics in complex, disordered quantum or classical systems.
